# Running `toolkit` commands

Purpose: how to run a `toolkit` command in Claude Code and in Codex, how to
pass text in one, and what each exit code means. Every skill that runs a
`toolkit` command follows this file.

## Contents

- Running toolkit commands
- Text in a command
- Exit codes
- Reporting a save
- Reading output and updating what you read
- Right and wrong examples

## Running toolkit commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- Why, in Codex: the project's command rule (`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules`)
  runs a `toolkit` command outside the sandbox only when it is the whole
  command. A `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion, the
  local Hindsight server, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and
  `.memory/` from a worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong
  cause.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc; "Text in a command", below).
- Six commands ask the owner first, in both hosts, because they are hard or
  impossible to undo, or change every project on this computer:
  `toolkit machine-setup`, `toolkit memory delete`, `toolkit memory import`,
  `toolkit import`, `toolkit hindsight service install` or `start`, and
  `toolkit rule add --machine` or `toolkit rule update --machine` (write
  `--machine` right after `add` or `update`). Get his yes in the reply before
  you run one; his own words ("for all my projects, always ...") are that yes
  for a rule. The host then asks him to confirm the command (Claude
  Code: a permission prompt; Codex: an approval). That prompt is expected, not
  an error.
- When the host refuses one of the six without asking him (Codex with
  approvals off: "approval required by policy, but AskForApproval is set to
  Never"), say that the cause is that approval setting, show him the exact
  command to run himself in a terminal, and wait. Do nothing in its place
  that he did not ask for: a refused delete is not a retire.
- In Codex, run each of those six alone, with `sandbox_permissions` set to
  `require_escalated` and a one-line reason. The approval alone keeps the
  command inside the sandbox, where it fails: `toolkit memory delete` cannot
  reach Hindsight or Notion, `toolkit machine-setup` cannot write `~/.codex`
  or `~/.local/bin`, `toolkit hindsight service install` cannot write
  `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, `toolkit rule add --machine` cannot write
  `~/.claude/rules`, and `toolkit import` from a worktree cannot write the
  main checkout.
- Write `--json` and `--host` after the command words
  (`toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved --json`). The toolkit refuses
  those six commands when a flag comes first, because the ask-first rules
  would not match them.
- Never change a work item or a memory record with a script or a shell write
  (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`, `tee`, `cp`). Use the `toolkit` command
  that owns it. The hooks refuse the shell write, so it only wastes a step.
- `toolkit help <command>` prints every option of one command.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still reports success. So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Never use double quotes for text.
- **An apostrophe inside single quotes:**
  - Claude Code: write it as `'\''`, for example
    `--note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`.
  - Codex: write it as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the text.
    Never `'\''` in Codex: the command rule does not match that form, so the
    command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can drop the
    backslash, which leaves a quote that is never closed.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere.
  Claude Code refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary file there
  could never be deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line
  holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --set-file - <<'EOF'
  <the whole section text>
  EOF
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text:
  1. Make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d`. Its name is
     unique, so two sessions or two projects never share a file.
  2. Write the file in it with the file edit tool (`apply_patch`).
  3. Run the `toolkit` command alone, with the file's full path.
  4. Delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds
     (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything.

  Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
  ```

- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`. Every
  project starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this
  item.
- Never leave a draft file inside `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. A second
  `DESIGN.md`-shaped file there confuses the design lookup, and a stray note
  in `.memory/` is read as a memory.

## Exit codes

`toolkit help work` prints them as: "0 ok, 1 error, 2 validation failure or a
refused gate, 3 not supported for this tracker, 4 not a toolkit project."
`toolkit help memory` uses the same numbers: "1 error or not found, 2 refused
(a rule or a stale --expect), 3 not supported by this backend".

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Done. | Read back what you wrote before you report it as saved ("Reporting a save", below). A "Note:" line in the output still needs action: report it to the owner, or do what it says. |
| `1` | Error, or the record was not found. | Read the message. It names the cause and usually the fix. Do not run the same command again unchanged. |
| `2` | Validation failure, a refused gate, or a stale `--expect`. | Fix what the message names and run the command again. A refused gate means an approval is missing: ask the owner for it. Never work around a refusal. |
| `3` | Not supported for this tracker or memory backend. | For a GitHub or Jira tracker, the message prints the path of the written instructions for that tracker. Follow them to make the same change on the issue. |
| `4` | Not a Toolkit V2 project. | Skip every work item and memory step and say so in one line. To set the project up, open the `project-setup` skill. |

`toolkit: command not found` means this computer cannot reach the command.
The `project-setup` skill fixes that.

## Reporting a save

- Save each settled answer before moving on, then read it back. A command
  that exits `0` is not proof by itself.
- A write failed: lead the reply with "Not saved". Name what was not saved
  and where it should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- "Saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first part that differs. Lead the
  reply with "Saved but not verified", say which part, and read the record
  back to judge it.

## Reading output and updating what you read

- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field, for example
  a record's `version`.
- `--expect <version>` tells the command which version of a record you read.
  The command refuses the save (exit `2`) when the record changed since then,
  so you never overwrite a newer edit. Read it again, merge, and save with the
  new version. `toolkit memory focus`, `toolkit memory glossary`, and
  `toolkit memory save` take it. `--expect absent` says it must not exist
  yet: a new record, or a project with no focus yet.

## Right and wrong examples

1. Two reads.
   - Wrong: `toolkit work list && toolkit work show WI-004`
   - Right: `toolkit work list`, then, as a second command,
     `toolkit work show WI-004`.
2. A history note that quotes the owner, with an apostrophe in his words.
   - Wrong: ``toolkit work history WI-004 --note "Owner said: it's ready, `ship it`"``
     (double quotes: the shell runs the words between the backticks as a
     command and saves its output in their place).
   - Right in Claude Code:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`
   - Right in Codex:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it’s ready, ship it"'`
   - The prefix is `Owner said:`, which has no apostrophe to escape.
3. Section text in Codex.
   - Wrong: `cat > /tmp/overview.md <<'EOF' ... EOF && toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --set-file /tmp/overview.md`
     (one shell command, a heredoc, and a fixed file name).
   - Right: `toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'`
4. A change to a work item's header.
   - Wrong: `sed -i '' 's/^stage: .*/stage: 04-solution-design/' .work-items/WI-004/WORK-ITEM.md`
   - Right: `toolkit work set WI-004 --stage 04-solution-design --note '<why>'`
5. Toolkit commands from a script.
   - Wrong: `for id in WI-001 WI-002; do toolkit work show $id; done`
   - Right: `toolkit work show WI-001`, then `toolkit work show WI-002`, each
     as its own command.

# Work item and design format

What a work item and its design hold, their exact section names, and how to
change them with `toolkit work` commands without losing text.

## Contents

1. Where the record and the design live
2. Header fields
3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`
4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`
5. Finding an item's file
6. Changing one section
7. Adding a table row
8. Editing a record directly
9. Titles
10. Generated files
11. Examples

## 1. Where the record and the design live

Every tracker uses the same body and the same design shape. Only the place
differs.

| Tracker | Work item | Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local | `WORK-ITEM.md` in the item's folder under `.work-items/` | `DESIGN.md` beside it |
| Notion | The item's page in the project's Work Items database | The item's "Solution Design" child page |
| GitHub Issues | The issue body | One issue comment whose first line is `## Solution design` |
| Jira | The issue description | One comment whose first line is "Solution design" |

An item has one design home. Never make a separate design folder or a second
design file.

## 2. Header fields

The header (frontmatter locally, properties in Notion) holds these fields.
Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

| Field | Values | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `WI-001` (the project's prefix and a number) | `toolkit work new`; never reused |
| `title` | The owner's words for the request | `toolkit work set <id> --title` |
| `type` | `discovery`, `solution-design`, `build`, `data-load`, `repository-maintenance`, `research`, `task`, `bug`, `enhancement`, or another lower-case word | `toolkit work set <id> --type` |
| `stage` | `01-discovery` to `14-spec-update` | `toolkit work set <id> --stage`, `approve`, `finish`, `cancel` |
| `status` | Backlog, Ready, In Progress, In Review, Done, Cancelled | Follows the stage; Done and Cancelled only through `finish` and `cancel` |
| `parent` | An item id or `none` | `toolkit work new --parent`, `toolkit work move` |
| `waiting_on` | `owner`, `agent`, `external: <who>`, `none` | `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on` |
| `priority` | `urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low` | `toolkit work set <id> --priority` |
| `delivery` | `agent-led`, `owner-led`, `not-offered` | `toolkit work set <id> --delivery` |
| `requirements_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements` |
| `design` | `proposed`, `approved`, `superseded`, `none` | `toolkit work design`, `toolkit work approve <id> --design` |
| `result_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --result`, `toolkit work finish --quote` |
| `updated` | `YYYY-MM-DD` | Every `toolkit work` write |

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stage labels, the statuses, and the types.
Blocked is not a status: an item that cannot move has `waiting_on` set and its
Overview Blockers line filled.

## 3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` takes. A `###` subsection can be named on
its own, for example `--section 'Agreed goal'`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | The phase table: Phase (`P1 — <name>`), Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | One `### P1 — <name>` heading per phase, with checkbox tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: Date, Change or decision, Effect on the work (newest first) |
| `Open Questions` | Rows: ID (`Q-01`), Question, Affects, Status, Decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status and Finalization rule, then the subsections below |
| `Starting request` | The owner's own words for the request |
| `Agreed goal` | The outcome the owner agreed the item delivers |
| `Active requirements` | One `#### R-01 — <name>` block per requirement |
| `Acceptance` | The numbered list of what makes the whole item acceptable |
| `Notes` | The subsections below |
| `Decisions and context` | Context the next session needs that is not a requirement |
| `Resume here` | Where the next session picks up |
| `Solution options and considerations` | Build ideas, linked to an `R-xx`; never requirements |

The `R-xx` block fields are Status (Refining, Finalized, Superseded), Applies
to, Required behavior, Boundaries and exceptions, Acceptance check, Decision
record, and Open questions. Each field starts its own line.

In the local and Notion trackers, the requirements approval command sets the
Requirements "Overall status" line: never write that line by hand there.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Finalized there itself (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`,
"The `toolkit work` steps").

## 4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`

The CLI writes the design's header fields: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what is left to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C), each with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow; Components and responsibilities; Data, access, and integration details; Edge cases and failure behavior; Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep every heading exactly as the template has it, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`. In the local and Notion trackers, never write "Approved"
in the Design status line: a save replaces that line with the stored status,
and only `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>` approves a design.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Approved there itself (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`).

## 5. Finding an item's file

Never build a path by hand. The owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

```text
toolkit work show <id> --path
```

`toolkit work show <id>` also prints the item's stage, who it waits on, the
skill that continues it, its parent and sub-items, its design (or the
parent's approved design it inherits), and the worktree branch and folder to
use.

## 6. Changing one section

1. Read the section. The output is the whole section as it stands.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section '<heading>'`
2. Change only what needs to change. Keep the rest word for word.
3. Leave out the section's fill-in guide comment (`<!-- ... -->`) once the
   section holds real content.
4. Write the whole section back. `<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the text
   on standard input; in Codex use `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new
   `mktemp -d` folder (`toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section '<heading>' --set-file <file>`
5. Read it back. An exit code of `0` is not proof by itself.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section '<heading>'`

To remove the template's fill-in guide above Overview:

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --remove-guide
```

## 7. Adding a table row

Add one row to Open Questions or Recent History with `--append-row` and the
full Markdown row in single quotes.

A new question takes the next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions
section first and add one to the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is
none). "Decision needed from" is `owner` for the owner, or a person or role.
When you asked it with a recommendation, the Question cell holds both:
the question, then "Recommended: <answer>, because <reason>."

```text
toolkit work show <id> --section 'Open Questions'
toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| Q-03 | Should the export include archived rows? | R-02 | Open | owner |'
```

A history row is added with its own command, which writes the date:

```text
toolkit work history <id> --note '<what happened>' --effect '<what it changes>'
```

To answer a question, rewrite its row in the whole Open Questions section:
the answer, the date, and status Answered. An approve command or a
`--delivery` answer marks the rows that asked for it Answered by itself and
prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; do not edit those rows again.

## 8. Editing a record directly

- Prefer `toolkit work edit`. It works in every tracker the CLI drives and
  keeps the CLI's record of what it wrote.
- A local record's body text may also be changed with the file edit tool. The
  post-tool hook checks the record after the edit.
- Never change the header fields with a file edit, and never create a record
  with one. The pre-tool hook refuses both, because they would skip the
  approval gates.
- Never write a record from the shell: no `cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`, `cp`, and
  no Python or Node script. The hook refuses it, so it only wastes a step.
- A Notion item changes only through `toolkit work` commands. Never write its
  page with another Notion tool.

## 9. Titles

- A new item's title uses the owner's own words for the request. When you
  shorten them, say the title in one line in the reply ("I started WI-003,
  'Write a short project brief'.").
- To retitle an item, say the new title to the owner in one line first. Never
  retitle quietly.
  `toolkit work set <id> --title '<new title>'`

## 10. Generated files

Never edit these by hand or from the shell. The hooks refuse it.

- `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md`: rebuilt by every `toolkit work` write and by
  `toolkit work sync`.
- `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`: the id-to-path map and the highest id
  used.

## 11. Examples

An Open Questions row for a content question the owner must answer:

```markdown
| Q-01 | What should the project brief cover: goals only, or goals, users, and scope? Recommended: goals, users, and scope, because the build needs all three. | P1-T01 | Open | owner |
```

A history note that records an owner's answer and says what it changes:

```text
toolkit work history WI-012 --note 'Owner said: "keep archived rows out of the export"' --effect 'R-02 updated; requirements approval asked again.'
```

A section edit in Claude Code: the command, then the text, then a line holding
only `EOF`, all in one shell command:

```text
toolkit work edit WI-012 --section 'Agreed goal' --set-file - <<'EOF'
Anyone on the team can export the monthly report as a CSV file that opens in Excel.
EOF
```

The same edit in Codex:

```text
toolkit work edit WI-012 --section 'Agreed goal' --text 'Anyone on the team can export the monthly report as a CSV file that opens in Excel.'
```

# Sizing a request and routing an item

How `work-on` decides between a quick edit, a logged item, and a worked item,
which type to give it, and which skill continues it.

## Contents

1. Three sizes of request
2. Owner messages and the right action
3. Choosing the type
4. Routing by where the item stands
5. Several items at once
6. Project roadmap units

## 1. Three sizes of request

- **Quick edit, no item.** One sitting, no choice for the owner, no change to
  behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production. Do it
  and report it in one line.
- **Log only.** The owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or
  "log a bug". Check the list for a duplicate, create the item at
  `01-discovery` with his exact words as the Starting request, reply
  "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop.
- **Work item.** Everything else. "New work", "track", "work item", or "done
  properly" always makes an item. A request that grows past a quick edit
  while you work becomes an item then, with his words as the Starting
  request.

Never make a work item for project setup. Setup steps the owner must do go in
the reply. Only a step `toolkit doctor` checks (trusting the hooks in Codex
`/hooks`, `ntn login`) also goes in the current focus under "Waiting on the
owner", marked as a setup step, and leaves it once doctor stops reporting it.
"Start a new session" goes in the reply only.

A deliverable the owner named without saying what it should say or do ("write
a short project brief"): create the item, add the content question as `Q-01`
with the item waiting on him, and ask it in the reply before building.
Never invent the content.

## 2. Owner messages and the right action

| The owner says | Right action |
| --- | --- |
| "Fix the typo in the README heading." | Quick edit. Fix it, say what changed in one line. No item. |
| "What does the export function do?" | Answer the question. No item. |
| "Log a bug: the export drops the last row. Not now." | Log only: check for a duplicate, create a `bug` item at `01-discovery` with his words, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." |
| "Add a CSV export to the monthly report." | Work item, type `build`. Create it, then route: requirements are not approved, so open `work-requirements`. |
| "Write a short project brief." | Work item, type `task`. Add `Q-01` "What should the brief cover?", set it waiting on the owner, ask the question. |
| "Keep going." (no item named) | Continue this worktree's item, or the item the current focus says the next session starts with, or the one `toolkit work next` recommends. Say which in one line. |
| "ok" (and this chat asked him nothing) | Not "keep going". Start no work; ask what he wants. |
| "Ask me questions first, then build it." | Create the item and open `work-requirements` for the interview. Never batch questions here. |
| "Put it in the backlog and I'll tell you when." | Log only. |
| "WI-007" or "resume WI-007" | Read WI-007 and route it by where it stands (section 4). |

## 3. Choosing the type

- Pick the closest type from `toolkit work lifecycle`.
- A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`),
  or to anything bound for production is `build`, never `task`, even when it
  looks small. A change to data is `data-load`.
- `build` and `data-load` need the owner's requirements approval before stage
  03. The CLI refuses a later stage without it.
- A `task` with no open choices may skip the requirements approval and go
  straight to planning. Put the reason in a history note.

## 4. Routing by where the item stands

The "Continue with" line of `toolkit work show <id>` is the default. The
item's real state decides. Go down the table in order and take the first row
that matches: the owner's waiting decisions come first, then the delivery
offer, then the stage. Say the route in one line.

| Where the item stands | Open | One-line announcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `waiting_on: owner` | `work-decide` (ask that one question first; keep working on anything it does not block) | "WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements." |
| The agent to-do "Make the agent-led delivery offer" for this item (the briefing and `toolkit work decisions` list it for a big top-level item at stages 03 to 07 that still has `delivery: not-offered`), or the owner hands the goal over ("you drive") | `work-delegate`, and build nothing until he answers | "WI-012 needs your delivery choice; opening work-delegate." |
| Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load` | `work-requirements` | "WI-012 needs requirements first; opening work-requirements." |
| The owner asks to change, add, or drop a requirement, at any stage | `work-requirements` | "That changes R-02; opening work-requirements." |
| Requirements approved, more than one reasonable way to build, no approved design | `solution-design` | "WI-012 needs a design; opening solution-design." |
| Requirements approved, one clear way to build, no design | Stay here: say the approach in the final reply ("One way to build this: <approach>. I'll build it that way; say 'design first' to stop me.") and put the reason in a history note | |
| Too big for one build | `work-organize` (split, stage 05) | "WI-012 is too big for one build; opening work-organize." |
| Design approved, or a sub-item that inherits the parent's approved design | Stay here: plan (stage 06) | |
| Stages 09 to 11 | `work-check` | "WI-012 is in testing; opening work-check." |
| Stages 12 to 14, or result approved | `work-finish` | "WI-012 is approved; opening work-finish." |
| Done or Cancelled | Nothing. Reopen only when the owner asks: `toolkit work set <id> --stage <s> --reopen` | |

- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a one-line reason
  when a move is not obvious.
- An item that changes committed files always goes through stage 07 (its own
  worktree). Never build on the default branch.
- A worktree whose branch names an item (`claude/wi-007-csv-export`) belongs
  to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in.

## 5. Several items at once

- Read each item's record before recommending an order. Say what can go
  ahead on its own, what depends on another outcome, and which one decision
  would unblock the most work.
- Each item has one main session that changes it. Other sessions return
  findings to it instead of editing the same record.
- Worktrees keep code apart; they do not keep shared environments apart.
  Check shared orgs, databases, and releases before two items change the same
  one.

## 6. Project roadmap units

`PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized
work units, each naming its work item id. Item detail stays in the tracker.

- When a new item is one of those units, write its id into the unit and save
  the file with `publish-docs`.
- An item's own phases (`P1`) are a different thing. They live in the item's
  Roadmap section.

# Recording the owner's answers

Where each thing the owner says is saved, how to ask him a question, how to
end a reply, and what to say when a save fails.

## Contents

1. Voice
2. Where each answer goes
3. Save it before the next question
4. History notes
5. Waiting on the owner
6. Asking the owner
7. Ending every reply
8. Reporting a failed save
9. Owner edits win
10. Stages in plain words
11. Handing over to another skill

## 1. Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Helper agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file carries its
own writing rules.

## 2. Where each answer goes

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Active requirements` (the `R-xx` block) and `Acceptance` | The new meaning, and Status Refining until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question and your recommendation, what it affects, Open, who must answer |
| Answer or decision about this item | The question's row, the section it changes, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| Context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to |
| A lasting fact, or why a part of the project exists or how it is used ("remember that the split is for my Friday dinners") | Project memory, through `memory-save`: the `project_` concept for that part, even while this item is open; the item may link to it | One section |
| An instruction for how the agent works ("from now on", "always", "never", a preference, a correction) | The rules, through `memory-save` (`toolkit rule add`) | One rule line |

A choice about how agents deliver a goal (the delivery offer) is recorded
only by `work-delegate`.

## 3. Save it before the next question

- Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
  unanswered question is also information: save it as an Open Questions row.
- Open decisions never delay saving answers that are already settled.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.
- Check the item and memory before asking the owner something. Never ask
  again what the record already answers.
- When two sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Never pick the
  convenient answer.

## 4. History notes

Add one note when:

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who; do not claim you checked
  it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

```text
toolkit work history <id> --note '<what happened>' --effect '<what it changes>'
```

- Without `--effect`, the row names the skill that continues the item. A note
  that quotes the owner right after an approval or a `waiting_on` change
  needs its own `--effect`: the default is worked out from the item before the
  change and can name the wrong next step.
- Record the owner's meaning briefly. Add no reason, scope, or certainty he
  did not give.
- A note that quotes him starts with `Owner said:`, followed by his words in
  double quotes inside the single-quoted text. A quote is his exact words:
  never reword it to avoid an apostrophe ("she'll" stays "she'll", never
  "she will").
- Keep apostrophes out of your own words in the note where you can. In a
  quote, and wherever one is needed, write it as `'\''` in Claude Code and as
  ’ (U+2019) in Codex (`toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs, or small
  edits.

Examples:

```text
toolkit work history WI-012 --note 'Owner said: "yes, approved"' --effect 'Requirements approved; solution-design continues.'
toolkit work history WI-012 --note 'Build found the export API has a 10,000-row limit.' --effect 'P2 added for paged exports.'
```

## 5. Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask him for an approval, or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
  `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
- `toolkit work approve` sets `waiting_on` from `owner` to `none`, because he
  just answered. Then set it to `agent` when the agent continues.
  `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- After he answers his last open question on the item: `agent` when the agent
  can continue, `none` when nothing waits. Keep `owner` while another of his
  questions on that item is still open.
- An item at `owner` stays in the briefing and in `toolkit work decisions`,
  and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of its next stage.
- Waiting on someone else: `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on 'external: <who>'`
  and the Overview Blockers line names what is missing.

## 6. Asking the owner

- Ask in the reply text. Never ask through a question tool (such as Codex's
  `request_user_input`): he may never see it, and the reply must hold the
  question.
- One question per message. Give your recommended answer and the main reason
  in one line, so he can confirm, correct, or redirect it.
- A question you cannot record an answer to yet gets an Open Questions row,
  and the recommendation goes in the row's Question cell, after the
  question, for example "Which input rule? Recommended: bills of 0 or more
  with at most two decimals, because ...". A later session then knows what
  "go with your recommendation" means. When a row has no recommendation and he says "go
  with your recommendation", say you cannot find the one he saw, give yours,
  and ask; never present a new recommendation as the one he approved.
- The one exception: more than three findings from the `work-requirements`
  spec check go in one numbered list he can answer in one message.
- Never ask him which stage an item is in, or which helpers a small item
  needs. Work those out yourself.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not an
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.

## 7. Ending every reply

End every reply to the owner with one of these:

- the one question he must answer ("Do you approve these requirements?");
- the exact words that continue the work ("Say 'keep going' and I'll start
  the build.").

Never end on "The next step is ..." with nothing for him to do.

## 8. Reporting a failed save

- The write failed: lead with "Not saved". Name what was not saved and where
  it should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified", name the line the CLI says differs, and read the item back to
  judge it.
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## 9. Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move or rename a folder, drag a
Notion card, change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, writes a history row,
and reports it. Never undo it.

- The session briefing lists these under "Changes found in the tracker", and
  every `toolkit work` command prints the ones it finds. Tell the owner each
  one in one line in the reply (not only in a progress line), before other
  work. Each line the CLI prints is written to be said as it is. Do not guess
  at a cause the CLI does not name.
- The CLI writes the history rows for a hand move. Add a note only for what it
  cannot know, such as the owner's reason.
- A hand change that skips a gate (a `build` item moved past stage 03 without
  approved requirements, or Done with no recorded result approval) is asked
  about as a question. The CLI prints the question and the command for each
  answer.

## 10. Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`: "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item waits for.

## 11. Handing over to another skill

- Claude Code: open the skill with the Skill tool, by name.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path in the skill list, then
  follow it.
- Say the handover in one line: "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`. The
  delivery offer is the exception: only `work-delegate` records it.

# Planning and building a work item

The Roadmap and Tasks formats, tracking setup, and the build rules for
`work-on` stages 06 to 08.

## Contents

1. Roadmap and tasks
2. The Roadmap format
3. The Tasks format
4. Status words and ticking a task
5. Tracking setup (stage 07)
6. Building (stage 08)
7. Keeping the item current while building
8. Checklist before stopping

## 1. Roadmap and tasks

- The Roadmap is an ordered list of phases from where the item stands to the
  finished result. Name phases to fit the work. "Phase" (`P1`) is the item's
  plan; "stage" (`08-build`) is the lifecycle. Never mix the two words.
- Build the phases from the approved design's "Build and verification plan"
  (its Technical sequence and Acceptance checks) and the chosen option's
  Build order. With no design (a small item that skipped design with a
  recorded reason), build them from the requirements.
- A sub-item that inherits its parent's approved design is planned from the
  parent's design: `toolkit work design <parent-id>`.
- Each phase has one or more tasks, one or more sub-items, or both.
- Keep detail in proportion. A one-hour fix needs one phase with one or two
  tasks.
- Link sources; do not copy them. A task names the `R-xx` it implements and
  the design section it follows.

## 2. The Roadmap format

The table keeps these columns in every tracker. The phase name follows an em
dash, as in the template.

```markdown
A phase is complete when its tasks are complete and its exit result has been checked.

| Phase | Outcome | Status | Exit result | Sub-items |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 — CSV export button | The export button creates a file | In Progress | The file opens in Excel with every column | None. |
| P2 — Large exports | Exports over 10,000 rows finish | Not Started | A 50,000-row export finishes in under a minute | WI-015 |
```

## 3. The Tasks format

Each phase gets a `###` heading with the same phase id and name as its
Roadmap row. Each task field (`**Work:**`, `**Deliverable:**`,
`**Done when:**`, `**Depends on:**`) starts its own line, and every line of a
task but the last ends with two spaces, which Markdown reads as a line break.
Never run the fields together on one line.

```markdown
### P1 — CSV export button

- [ ] **P1-T01 — Add the export endpoint** · In Progress  
  **Work:** Add the endpoint that streams the report rows as CSV (R-01, design Technical sequence step 1).  
  **Deliverable:** The endpoint and its tests.  
  **Done when:** The endpoint test passes and a manual export opens in Excel.  
  **Depends on:** None.
- [ ] **P1-T02 — Add the Export button** · Not Started  
  **Work:** Add the button that calls the endpoint (R-01).  
  **Deliverable:** The button and its test.  
  **Done when:** Clicking Export downloads the file.  
  **Depends on:** P1-T01.
```

Save both sections with the section command (`work-item-format.md`,
"Changing one section"):

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>
toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>
```

## 4. Status words and ticking a task

- Phase status: Not Started, In Progress, Done (Cancelled for a phase that
  was dropped). Use no other word, such as "Planned".
- Task status: Not Started, In Progress, Done, Cancelled.
- From stage 07 on, `toolkit work validate` warns when the Roadmap has no
  phase table, when Tasks has no checkbox lines, and when a template example
  row or task is left.
- Tick a task (`- [x]`, status Done) only with evidence: the test result
  line, the commit, or what the owner saw.
- A done or cancelled task is not reopened. Add a new task instead.
- A task whose "Done when" names the owner (for example "the owner confirms
  the wording") is not ticked by the agent. It becomes an Open Questions row
  with `owner` as who decides.
- A phase that a sub-item delivers lists the sub-item id in its Sub-items
  column. Finishing the sub-item does not finish or approve the parent.
- When the item is finished, every phase it completed says Done.

## 5. Tracking setup (stage 07)

Only what the item needs:

- **Branch and worktree** for code work: the worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, as the project's
  `.claude/rules/shared-repository-work.md` says. `toolkit work show <id>`
  prints the exact names. For WI-007:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`
  In Codex this Git write needs the owner's approval and escalated
  permissions (`git-rules.md`).
- **Salesforce projects:** the item's deployment folder
  `delivery/deployment/<work-item-id>-<short-name>/`, copied from
  `delivery/deployment/work-item-deployment-template/` and kept current by
  `sf-component-tracker`.
- **A test plan**, when the checks need more than the item's acceptance
  checks (several scenarios, a manual check, or a release): `work-check`
  writes it, in `tests/` on the item's branch.
- **Sub-items** for phases that own real scope: open `work-organize`.

## 6. Building (stage 08)

- Work on the item's own branch and worktree. Never on the default branch.
- One task at a time, in the order the Depends on lines allow.
- Commit with files staged by name and a plain message. No `Co-Authored-By`
  line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line (`git-rules.md`).
- With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per

### Active requirements

#### R-01 — Calculate the late fee

**Status:** Finalized  
**Applies to:** An overdue invoice amount and the number of days late supplied to the command.  
**Required behavior:** Calculate the late fee as 0.25% of the original invoice amount for each day late. Round the fee to the nearest cent, with half a cent rounded up. The total due is the invoice amount plus that rounded fee.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** Valid invoice amounts are $0 or more with at most two decimal places. Valid day counts are whole numbers of 0 or more. Missing or invalid inputs do not produce a calculated total.  
**Acceptance check:** For an invoice amount of $200 and 10 days late, the fee is $5.00 and the total due is $205.00. For an invoice amount of $1 and 2 days late, the half-cent fee rounds up to $0.01 and the total due is $1.01. A missing or invalid amount or day count produces no calculated total.  
**Decision record:** Mike Rihm, 2026-09-29, starting request, rounding answer, input rule answer, missing or invalid input answer, total due answer, and approval of WI-001 requirements.  
**Open questions:** None.

#### R-02 — Print the dollar amounts

**Status:** Finalized  
**Applies to:** A command run with an invoice amount and the days-late option.  
**Required behavior:** For valid input, print one line containing the late fee and total due in dollars, each with two decimal places. For missing or invalid input, print a clear error to standard error, exit unsuccessfully, and print no total.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** No second line is requested unless the cents option is supplied.  
**Acceptance check:** For an invoice amount of $200 and 10 days late, the first line is exactly "Late fee: $5.00  Total due: $205.00". A run with a missing or invalid input prints a clear error on standard error, exits unsuccessfully, and prints no total.  
**Decision record:** Mike Rihm, 2026-09-29, starting request, missing or invalid input answer, and approval of WI-001 requirements.

**Status:** Finalized

**Boundaries and exceptions:** The cents value must represent the invoice amount plus the rounded fee, matching the total due shown in dollars.

66:#### Technical shape
67-
68-- `bin/feecalc.js` is the CLI entry point. A small set of local functions can handle argument parsing, amount parsing, fee computation, and formatting; a separate module is unnecessary for this one command.
69-- Proposed amount grammar: `^\+?(?:[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]{0,2})?|\.[0-9]{1,2})$`. Proposed days grammar: `^\+?[0-9]+$`. These accept common spellings of R-01's valid values; R-01 does not specify token spelling. Validate text before constructing either `BigInt` to avoid uncaught parsing exceptions and accidental acceptance of exponent notation or invalid precision.
70-- The amount parser removes an optional leading `+`, splits on `.`, supplies `0` for a missing whole or fractional part, pads the fractional portion on the right, and builds integer cents. The days parser constructs one `BigInt` from the validated token.
71-- Compute `product = amountCents * days`; `feeCents = product / 400n + (product % 400n >= 200n ? 1n : 0n)`; `totalCents = amountCents + feeCents`. No arithmetic path uses `Number`, including formatting.
72-- Format cents with `cents / 100n` for dollars and `(cents % 100n).toString().padStart(2, '0')` for cents.

# Work check

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Checks a finished build against every requirement with an independent checker, fixes what fails, and asks the owner to approve the result; it never merges, deploys, or marks Done. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does: the id he named, this worktree's item, or a title that matches; two matches, ask one question naming both. Read the requirements, the Acceptance list, the Tasks, and the design's Acceptance checks; a sub-item with no design of its own is checked against its parent's (`references/testing.md`, section 1). Then set the testing stage.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work design <id>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 09-testing`
2. Run the project's tests and every acceptance check the item lists. Several scenarios or manual steps: write a test plan in `tests/` on the item's branch (`references/testing.md`, sections 2 and 3).
3. Brief the `acceptance-checker`, never the agent that built it, naming the branch and the exact commit (`references/testing.md`, section 4). It runs before every result approval, whoever built the change (`references/helpers.md`, section 6).
4. Failures: run the check and fix loop until clean, or until a failure needs an owner decision (`references/testing.md`, section 5).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 10-bug-fixing`
5. Record what was checked, the checker's verdict, the evidence, and the gaps.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Checked: <what>; acceptance-checker: <its verdict>; evidence: <where>; gaps: <gaps or none>'`
6. Ask for the result approval with the checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 4: stage 11, the item waiting on the owner, the result shown as "Showing the result" says below, and one question: "Do you approve this result?"
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 11-user-approval --waiting-on owner`
7. His yes: save his words first, record the approval, hand the item back to the agent, and open `work-finish`. A requirement change goes to `work-requirements`; a fix becomes a task and continues here.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
8. Update the current focus when the item's next step changed (`references/current-focus.md`). End every reply with the approval question, or the exact words that continue.

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- The checker is never the agent or session that built the change. When no independent check could run, say so plainly before asking for approval.
- The `acceptance-checker` runs before every result approval (the owner's decision of 2026-09-28). "No agent team", "owner-led", "I'll lead it myself", or a no to the team question decide only who builds; they never remove it. Only when this host has no way to start a worker, check the result yourself and say plainly that no independent check ran, and why. If he asks to skip it, remind him of that decision and ask whether he wants to change it (`references/helpers.md`, section 6).
- The toolkit refuses the result approval (exit 2) until step 5's note with the checker's verdict is recorded after the last build. Record the note first. `--no-independent-check --reason '<why no worker could start>'` is only for a host that cannot start a worker, and the reason goes in the history.
- The change is only in a worktree until it is merged. When the reply gives him a command to try, name the worktree folder and give the command with its folder, for example `cd <worktree path>` first.
- A check that did not run is reported as not run, never as passed.
- The test plan lives in `tests/` on the item's branch, committed there. Never in `.work-items/`, which Git ignores.
- "Looks good" to any question other than the approval question is not the approval. Ask the approval question.
- Add no Open Questions row for the result approval: stage 11 already lists it as the owner's decision.
- When the approve command fails, show the owner its error. Never work around it by editing the record.
- The result approval covers the result shown, never merge, deployment, or publishing; `work-finish` handles those.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Change the stage label and record the result in the issue (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

## Showing the result

- Lead with what the result does now, in the owner's terms: "The export button now creates a CSV file that opens in Excel."
- Then how he can see it himself: the link, the command to run, or a screenshot.
- Then the evidence: tests run and their result lines, the checker's verdicts.
- Then the gaps: anything partly met, not run, or known to be missing. Never hide a gap to get an approval.
- One question: "Do you approve this result?"

A "no": record his words, turn each named problem into a task or a requirement change, and continue.

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`): step 3 and every re-check.
- `builder` (`references/agent-builder.md`): fixes in step 4 when a team was recorded or the owner agreed; one builder per independent fix, one writer per path. In Codex the main agent first makes each builder's worktree (`references/helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders").
- Brief them as `references/helpers.md` says.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. # Acceptance checker

Check whether a finished result does what the owner asked. You are never the
agent that built it. You run tests and read code, but you change nothing. You
advise; the main agent fixes; the owner approves.

## Contents

- Start with the brief
- Check
- Plan check (only when the brief asks for one)
- Boundaries
- Return (result check)
- Writing

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the requirements (Agreed goal, every
  `R-xx` with its acceptance check, the Acceptance list), the design's
  Acceptance checks table (in its "Build and verification plan") and the
  "How to check it" column of the selected option's Requirement coverage, the
  item's test plan when it has one (a copy of `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md`),
  the branch or commit to check, and the project's test commands.
- Check that you are looking at the exact code the brief names:

  ```text
  git status
  git rev-parse HEAD
  git log --oneline -5
  ```

  If the commit differs from the one in the brief, say so first.
- When the brief asks for a check before a merge, report the exact commit
  you checked, so the main agent can confirm nothing changed after it.

## Check

- Run the project's tests and every acceptance check you can run. Copy each
  command and its result line exactly.
- For each requirement, give one verdict:
  - **Met:** the acceptance check passed, or the evidence shows the required
    behavior. Name the evidence.
  - **Partly met:** some of the behavior works. Say what is missing.
  - **Not met:** the behavior is missing or wrong. Say what you saw.
  - **Not run:** the check could not run here. Say why and what would run it.
    Never report a check that did not run as passed.
- Read the diff for the item's branch against its base. Report defects you
  see: broken edge cases, missing error handling the requirements ask for,
  behavior the requirements did not ask for, files changed that the design
  did not name, and anything that would ship something unfinished.
- Walk the flow start to finish as the person who uses the result. Report any
  step where it breaks, even when each requirement passes on its own.

## Plan check (only when the brief asks for one)

Before a build starts, the brief may give the item's Roadmap and Tasks, the
requirements, and the design's "Build and verification plan" instead of a
finished result.
Then check the plan, not code:

- Every `R-xx` is covered by at least one task, and every task's "Done when"
  names evidence someone else can check.
- Each task has one owner, and each file has one writer. "Depends on" is
  right: no task starts before what it needs.
- Tasks that run at the same time have clear boundaries: no two builders
  write the same file, and no two use the same shared environment (a sandbox
  org, a database, a test service) at the same time without a stated order.
- No task relies on something the design or the code no longer says.
- Changes that affect other work items are named.

A different phase structure is not a defect by itself. Work that runs in
parallel does not need one agent per phase. Return for a plan check: the
verdict (ready to build, or not ready) in one line, then each finding with
the task id, what is wrong, and the fix in one line.

## Boundaries

- Bash is for tests and read-only commands only: running tests, `git status`,
  `git diff`, `git log`, `git show`, listing files. Never edit, stage, commit,
  push, merge, deploy, install, or delete anything.
- Never run a command against a shared or production org or service. Never
  touch production data.
- Never run a `toolkit` command that writes. Do not edit the work item.
- Do not start other agents. Do not ask the owner anything.

## Return (result check)

1. **Verdict:** ready for the owner, or not ready, in one line, with the
   commit checked.
2. **Per requirement:** a table with the `R-xx`, the verdict, and the evidence
   or the gap in one line.
3. **Tests run:** each command and its exact result line.
4. **Defects in the diff:** each with the file and line, what is wrong, and
   the fix in one line. "None found" when there are none.
5. **Not run:** each check that could not run, and why.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every file, function, and setting.
Short sentences, one idea each. No figurative or metaphorical language, no
idioms, no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep
every number, path, and command output exactly as found. Lead with the
verdict and keep the report short. Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Testing a work item

How `work-check` decides what to check, writes a test plan when one is
needed, briefs the independent checker, runs the fix loop, and records the
result.

## Contents

1. What to check against
2. When a test plan is needed
3. Writing the test plan
4. Briefing the acceptance checker
5. The check and fix loop
6. Recording the result
7. Showing the result to the owner

## 1. What to check against

Read these before running anything:

- every `R-xx` block and its Acceptance check, and the item's Acceptance
  list: `toolkit work show <id>`;
- the design's "Build and verification plan" > Acceptance checks, and the
  selected option's "How to check it" column: `toolkit work design <id>`
  (it exits 1 when the item has no design);
- a sub-item whose show output says "Design: none of its own; WI-012's design
  is approved" is checked against the parent's design:
  `toolkit work design <parent-id>`;
- the Tasks section, to know what was built and on which branch.

## 2. When a test plan is needed

A test plan is needed when a check has several scenarios, a manual step, test
data, or a release across environments. The item's own acceptance checks are
enough when each one is a single automated test or a single observation.

## 3. Writing the test plan

- [ ] Work in the item's worktree, on its branch. Never on the default branch.
- [ ] Copy `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md` to `tests/<id>-TEST-PLAN.md`, for
      example `tests/WI-012-TEST-PLAN.md`. Leave the template unchanged.
- [ ] Fill it as its guide comment says: Scope (the `R-xx` and items
      checked), Environment and data, one Checks row per scenario, then
      Results and follow-up. Delete the guide and the example row.
- [ ] Commit it on the item's branch with the results filled in, staged by
      name (`git-rules.md`).
- [ ] Never save it in `.work-items/`: Git ignores that folder, so the plan
      would never be committed.

One Checks row:

```markdown
| A manager clicks Export on the September report | A CSV file downloads and opens in Excel with all 12 columns | Manual, in the staging app | tests/evidence/wi-012-export.png |
```

## 4. Briefing the acceptance checker

The checker is never the agent or session that built the change. It runs
before every result approval, whoever built the change: a delivery choice or
a no to the team question never removes it (`helpers.md`, section 6). Brief
the `acceptance-checker` (Claude Code: `work:acceptance-checker`; Codex: the
text of `references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`, given to a `spawn_agent`
worker with `fork_turns` set to `none`) with, pasted in:

1. The item id.
2. The Agreed goal, every `R-xx` with its acceptance check, and the
   Acceptance list.
3. The design's Acceptance checks and the "How to check it" column.
4. The test plan, when there is one.
5. The branch and the exact commit to check.
6. The job: "Return one verdict per requirement (met, partly met, not met)
   with evidence, defects seen in the diff, and checks that could not run.
   Flag only gaps that affect correctness or the stated requirements."
7. Files it may write: nothing.

## 5. The check and fix loop

Repeat until clean, or until a failure needs the owner:

- [ ] Run the project's tests and every acceptance check the item lists.
- [ ] Brief the checker, or brief it again after a fix, naming the new commit.
- [ ] A failure: set the bug-fixing stage, add a task for it, and fix it (a
      `builder` agent when a team was recorded or the owner agreed, otherwise
      the main agent).
      `toolkit work set <id> --stage 10-bug-fixing`
- [ ] Set the testing stage again and repeat.
      `toolkit work set <id> --stage 09-testing`
- [ ] Stop the loop when every requirement is met, or when a failure needs an
      owner decision: add an Open Questions row and set the item waiting on
      him.
- [ ] A failure that shows a requirement is wrong goes to `work-requirements`,
      never around it.

A check that did not run is reported as not run, never as passed.

## 6. Recording the result

One history note that says what was checked, the checker's verdict, where
the evidence is, and the gaps. The words `acceptance-checker:` in the note
are how `toolkit work` knows the check ran: without them, moving the item to
stage 11 or recording the result approval prints a note that no independent
check is recorded.

```text

```

When this host had no way to start a worker, write
`acceptance-checker: none, <why>` and say so to the owner first.

## 7. Showing the result to the owner

In this order:

1. What the result does now, in his terms: "The export button now creates a
   CSV file that opens in Excel."
2. How he can see it himself: the link, the command to run, or a screenshot.

# The current focus

Purpose: the format of the current focus, when to change it, and the exact
read-change-save sequence, in every memory backend.

## Contents

- What the focus is for
- The format
- What goes in each section
- When to check it
- Read, change, save
- A new project's focus
- Examples
- Checklist for a focus save

## What the focus is for

The current focus is the first thing the next session reads: the session
briefing includes it. It says what is happening now and where the next
session starts. It never repeats the tracker: a work item's status, tasks,
and history stay in the work item.

| Backend | Where the focus lives |
| --- | --- |
| Built-in | `.memory/CURRENT_FOCUS.md` in the main checkout |
| Hindsight | The document `focus` in the project's bank |
| Notion | The "Current focus" page under the project's page |

The same commands read and save it in every backend. Never edit the file or
the page by hand.

## The format

The model's format: a `# Current focus` title line, a `Last updated:` line,
then exactly four `##` sections in this order, under 50 lines in total.

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: <YYYY-MM-DD>, <source>, <person or agent>

## Now

## Waiting on the owner

## Untracked to-dos

## Next session starts with
```

What the command enforces:

- It refuses a focus that lacks one of the four sections, has another
  section, or is over 50 lines (exit code 2, nothing saved).
- It adds the title line or the `Last updated:` line when either is missing,
  and sets an older date to today. It cannot know the source or who wrote
  it, so write the line yourself.

## What goes in each section

- **Last updated:** the date, the source (for example `handoff`,
  `work-finish`, `chat`), and who wrote it (a person, or `agent`). Change it
  on every save.
- **Now:** the current outcome or area, with work item ids and titles only,
  for example `- WI-012 CSV export`. Never a status or a stage: the tracker
  holds those.
- **Waiting on the owner:** a decision or action only the owner can take
  that has no work item: what it is, who needs it, and when to check again.
  Work items that wait on him are listed by `toolkit work decisions`, not
  here. A setup step (trust the hooks in Codex, sign in to Notion with
  `ntn login`) stays only while `toolkit doctor` still reports it.
- **Untracked to-dos:** things the owner asked for that have no work item.
  When one becomes a work item, replace the line with the item's id under
  Now.
- **Next session starts with:** one entry: where to resume, what to read,
  and the next action. It is replaced at each handoff, not added to.
- Write "None." in a section with nothing in it.
- Keep it under 50 lines by replacing stale lines, never by appending. Never
  drop an owner to-do that is still open only to meet the limit.

## When to check it

Check the focus before the reply ends when:

- a work item's stage changes, or its next step changes to something the
  focus does not say. Check two things:
  1. Now lists the item (id and title). Add it when it is missing; take it
     off when the item is Done or Cancelled. For Done, take it off just
     before `toolkit work finish`, which backs up the focus as it is then.
  2. Next session starts with does not name a step that is done or no longer
     next. Replace that line with the item's real next step, in one line that
     points at the item, for example "Continue WI-012 from its Resume here:
     build P1."
- the owner asks for something with no work item (add it under Untracked
  to-dos), or a decision only he can make has no work item (Waiting on the
  owner).
- `toolkit doctor` no longer reports a setup step listed under Waiting on the
  owner (drop it).
- a session hands off (replace the one entry under Next session starts
  with).

Skip the save when nothing in the focus is wrong. Leave every line you are
not changing exactly as it is.

## Read, change, save

1. Read it with its version. The output has `text` and `version`:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --json
   ```

2. Change only the lines that need it, in the whole text, and update the
   `Last updated:` line.
3. Save the whole text with the version you read.
   Claude Code: `<file>` is `-`, with the text on standard input after a
   quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`), then a line holding only `EOF`.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>
   ```

   Codex: give the text in single quotes instead (newlines are kept), or
   use a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder and delete it after the save.
   Write an apostrophe as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the
   text. Never `'\''` in Codex: the project's command rule does not match
   that form, so the command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can
   drop the backslash.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
   ```

4. Exit code 2 with "changed since it was read" means another session saved
   the focus after you read it. Read it again, make your change in the new
   text, and save with the new version. Never save without `--expect`: that
   would silently drop the other session's change.
5. No focus yet (`version` is null): save with `--expect absent`, in the full
   format above.
6. Read it back:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus
   ```

## A new project's focus

A new project's focus still holds the model's setup text: a fill-in guide
comment under the title (`<!-- Fill-in guide: ... -->`) and an
`<angle-bracket>` prompt in every section. At the first save:

- remove the fill-in guide comment;
- replace each prompt with real content, or with "None." when there is none;
- never leave an angle-bracket prompt in a saved focus.

## Examples

A full focus:

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: 2026-09-26, handoff, agent

## Now

- WI-012 CSV export
- WI-015 Large exports (sub-item of WI-012)

## Waiting on the owner

- Pick a hosting provider before the first deploy (no work item yet); check again 2026-10-01.

## Untracked to-dos

- Email the client about the October demo.

## Next session starts with

- 2026-09-26 17:40 UTC | CSV export: continue WI-012 from its Resume here. Goal: exports finish under 10 seconds.
```

The handoff entry with a work item is a pointer only:
`<UTC date and time> | <topic>: continue <WI-id> from its Resume here. Goal: <one line>.`

With no work item, the entry is a short note: the goal or topic, where work
stopped, the first next action, limits on what may be done without the
owner, and open questions. Do not create a work item only to hold it.

## Checklist for a focus save

- [ ] Read with `--json`; you have the version.
- [ ] The `# Current focus` title and the `Last updated:` line (date,
      source, who) are there.
- [ ] Four sections, in order; "None." in each empty one.
- [ ] Work item ids and titles only; no status or stage.
- [ ] No angle-bracket prompt and no fill-in guide comment left.
- [ ] Under 50 lines; no open owner to-do dropped.
- [ ] Saved with `--expect`; read back.

# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics and read each one whole. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; the owner's instructions for how the agent works in `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md` (`toolkit rule add`); procedures in skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Keep one topic file per concept or area, such as `user_profile.md` or `project_billing.md`, with a `##` heading for each sub-topic and a last `## Gotchas and lessons` section for lessons not yet proven. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`; an `event` file holds one episode. The `feedback` prefix is retired: an older `feedback_` file is moved to the rules and concepts with `memory-tidy`. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Each file starts with its title, a one-line summary (`description`), and the date of its last change (`updated`). Aim for a quick read; split a topic that grows too large.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for the topic a new fact belongs to before creating one (`toolkit memory find`), and add the fact under a heading there (`toolkit memory save --concept <key> --section <heading>`). Create a new file only for a new concept. Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short line per active topic, grouped by prefix: its title, summary, and updated date, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a rule with `toolkit rule add`, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands, for example `save`, `retire`, `focus`, `glossary`, and `reindex` (`toolkit memory --help` lists them all). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. An instruction for how the agent works (a working preference, a correction, "from now on", "always", "never") is not memory: `memory-save` writes it to `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md` with `toolkit rule add`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, write the correction there as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those rules override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic: a new fact goes under a heading in the topic file for its concept, and a new file is only for a new concept. A lesson the agent learned and has not proven yet goes under the concept's "Gotchas and lessons" heading; when it recurs or the owner confirms it, the agent proposes it as a rule or a skill. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, or fact about the owner he stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details, a working preference or correction (a rule in `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md`) |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale (why a part of the project exists or how it is used), technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body, an instruction for how the agent works (a rule) |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode, one per file: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.
